title: Embrace the Willingness to Look Foolish
author: Parker Houston
summary: Parker Houston builds on an idea from Mark Batterson that the willingness to look foolish is a skill worth preserving, because as people age they grow more invested in appearing smart. He illustrates it with a plumber visit in which he was tempted to nod along at jargon, but instead asked basic questions and learned where the main shutoff valve is, how to isolate leaks, and how to adjust house water pressure. His conclusion is that the main obstacle to learning is often ego. He connects this to executive coaching, where a seemingly dumb question can break groupthink, as when a coach asked a client struggling with exercise why bother exercising at all and redirected the whole session. He applies the principle to parenting and to Jesus's call to become like little children, which he reads as humility and curiosity. He ends with five actions: ask a dumb question, practice until it is a habit, observe your ego, seek people who want to teach, and ask older people.
points: The willingness to look foolish is a learnable skill, and ego is often the only thing standing between a person and new knowledge.
Asking a basic question of an expert yields practical learning, because most experts want to pass on what they know.
Leaders and coaches who ask the dumb question can break groupthink and open new directions for a group.
Practical steps include asking one dumb question a week, watching your self-critical narrative, and seeking older people with decades of experience.
quotes: He suggested that the older we get, we lose this “ability,” and mostly become invested in looking smart to other people.
This incident helped me understand more clearly than ever before, that often the only thing standing in the way of learning, competence, and new knowledge—is me.

Those who are willing to let go of ego, set aside momentary embarrassment, and ask seemingly “dumb” questions, will eventually become much wiser and more knowledgeable than those who pretend to have all the answers, or try to preserve the image of appearing smart.
It’s amazing what happens when a coach asks a leader, or when a leader asks the team, the question that no one else is willing to ask because they are afraid of looking stupid.
Often, these “dumb” questions can snap a group out of groupthink, or generate new ways of looking at a problem.
Most people want to pass on their knowledge. In general, experts want to share their expertise and people want to pass along what they know.
It turns out that when you admit you are struggling and ask around, you can get some really life-changing tips!
Observe your ego. Practice watching your mind and noticing any self-critical narrative.
